content: Renal transplant patients are under immunosuppression to modulate the immune response to the transplanted organ. These patients often have underlying chronic kidney diseases and other comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension, which can influence the outcomes of COVID-19 infection. Consequently, they are at a higher risk of developing complications associated with COVID-19. The clinical manifestations, treatment, and prognosis of COVID-19 in renal transplant patients may differ from those in the general population. While the risk of donor-to-recipient transmission of the virus remains unknown, any transplant recipient exposed to the infection is believed to have a high likelihood of severe disease. The etiological agent responsible for COVID-19 is the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), first identified in Wuhan, China. On March 12, 2020, the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic. Historical data from the earlier SARS epidemic in Hong Kong showed that both pediatric and adult renal transplant patients were affected, with adult patients experiencing more severe disease. The first reported case of COVID-19 in a renal transplant patient was a 52-year-old man in Wuhan, China, who had received a kidney transplant 12 years earlier for chronic glomerulonephritis. He successfully recovered and was discharged on day 13 of hospitalization. The classification of COVID-19 infection in renal transplant patients depends on the severity of the disease, as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO). Pathophysiologically, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and dipeptidyl peptidase have been implicated in the uptake of SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV. The viral spike (S) protein interacts with the host ACE2 receptor, facilitating viral entry into human cells. ACE2 receptors are more abundant in the kidneys than in the respiratory system, particularly in the proximal tubules. The spike protein is cleaved and activated by the transmembrane serine protease family (TMPRSS) after binding to ACE2 receptors. Genetic factors, such as certain HLA alleles, may influence susceptibility to COVID-19 and the severity of complications. For instance, HLA-B46:01 is associated with reduced viral presentation to the immune system, while HLA-B15:03 is linked to a higher likelihood of developing immunity. Acute kidney injury (AKI) has been reported in COVID-19 patients, often accompanied by proteinuria and hematuria. Renal transplant patients appear to be at a higher risk of developing AKI compared to the general population. The mechanisms underlying AKI in COVID-19 include direct cytotropic effects of the virus on proximal tubule cells, systemic inflammatory responses driven by cytokines, and complications such as acute tubular necrosis (ATN), volume depletion, drug toxicity, and multiorgan failure. Elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and cytokine storms in severe cases can lead to immune-mediated damage to healthy tissues. Autopsy findings in COVID-19 patients have revealed macrophage infiltration in the tubulointerstitium, severe ATN, and complement deposition in renal tissues. The clinical features of COVID-19 in renal transplant patients may be atypical due to chronic immunosuppression. Common symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue, with some patients also experiencing diarrhea, lymphopenia, renal injury, and liver dysfunction. The severity of COVID-19 pneumonia in immunocompromised transplant patients compared to the general population remains to be fully elucidated. Data from China indicate that 81% of COVID-19 cases in the general population are mild, while 19% are severe or critical. In contrast, a study of renal transplant patients reported 80% severe cases, compared to 19% in the general population. Differentiating COVID-19 from other diseases presenting with similar symptoms, such as fever, cough, and shortness of breath, is crucial. COVID-19-associated AKI in renal transplant patients must also be distinguished from other causes of AKI, such as congestive heart failure, dehydration, urinary tract obstruction, and nephrotoxic medications. The incidence of COVID-19 in renal transplant patients is challenging to estimate due to limited testing and data. However, patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), those on chronic replacement therapies, and kidney transplant recipients are at increased risk. AKI has been observed in 5-15% of SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV infections. COVID-19-associated AKI is more prevalent in elderly patients in the general population. Men are more likely to be affected by COVID-19 than women, and women who die from the disease tend to be older than men. Racial disparities have also been noted, with higher proportions of Black and Hispanic patients among renal transplant recipients affected by COVID-19 in some studies. Risk factors for COVID-19 in renal transplant patients include immunosuppression, chronic renal failure, comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, heart disease), male sex, older age, smoking history, and potential donor-related infection. Screening for AKI in renal transplant patients involves serial monitoring of kidney function tests, including blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and urine analysis. Severe COVID-19 cases require additional measurements of D-dimer, ferritin, and troponin to screen for coagulopathies. Elevated inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), are common in severe cases. Management of immunosuppression in renal transplant patients with COVID-19 is complex and should be individualized based on factors such as age, disease severity, comorbidities, and time since transplantation. In mild to moderate cases, immunosuppressive drug doses may be reduced or continued, but this approach carries risks of graft rejection. Corticosteroids may be beneficial due to their immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties. Other immunosuppressive agents, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and azathioprine, are often discontinued during hospitalization. Tacrolimus doses may be reduced, and target levels should be maintained at 3-5 ng/mL. Cyclosporine A has shown inhibitory effects on coronavirus replication in vitro and may be considered, with target levels of 25-50 ng/mL. Tocilizumab, an anti-interleukin-6 monoclonal antibody, has been trialed in patients with cytokine storm and inflammation. Surgical interventions are not typically required for COVID-19 in renal transplant patients. Transplantation procedures should be delayed in infected candidates until clinical improvement and negative viral detection are confirmed. Preventive measures for renal transplant patients include adherence to general public health guidelines, such as mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing. Teleconsultations are recommended to minimize exposure to healthcare settings. Patients should maintain a healthy lifestyle, avoid smoking and alcohol, and follow a balanced diet. Infected patients should be tested 10-14 days after symptom onset and require two negative PCR tests at least 24 hours apart before being considered non-infectious.
